s1_definition.profdef: The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i−1 (then take a single step) plus the ways to reach step i−2 (then take a double step), so dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2] with base cases dp[0]=1 and dp[1]=1. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solvable bottom-up in linear time and constant space.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i−1 (then take a single step) plus the ways to reach step i−2 (then take a double step), so dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2] with base cases dp[0]=1 and dp[1]=1. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solvable bottom-up in linear time and constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer at National Bank of India climbs a rewards tier ladder one or two tiers at a time. The ways to reach a given tier is the ways to reach the tier just below (then step one) plus the ways to reach two tiers below (then step two). Add those and you have the count for every tier.

**One line to remember:** Ways to reach step i = ways to i−1 plus ways to i−2 — it's Fibonacci.

sections.s2_technical:
The last move into step i is either a single step from i−1 or a double step from i−2, and those two groups of paths are disjoint and cover all possibilities, so you add them. For example: `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2];`.

Base cases: there is one way to stand at the ground (do nothing) and one way to reach the first step. Iterating upward keeps only the last two values, since dp[i] depends on just the previous two. For example: `cur = prev1 + prev2; prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur;`.

The time is O(n) and the space is O(1) with the rolling variables. A senior nuance is that a generalized "climb up to k steps" variant sums the previous k values, which is the k-step Fibonacci and still linear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a loyalty ladder lets a member advance one or two tiers per action, and marketing wants to count the distinct progression paths to a target tier. This is exactly how Climbing Stairs works.

Problem 2 — Each count builds on the two preceding counts, so only the last two need to be kept. This is exactly the constant-space rolling computation.

The mini-project builds a `LoyaltyLadderCounter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input n is five.

Step 1: Base counts are one way for tier zero and one way for tier one.

Step 2: Tier two is one plus one equals two; tier three is two plus one equals three.

Step 3: Tier four is three plus two equals five; tier five is five plus three equals eight.

Step 4: The rolling variables held only the last two counts throughout, and the answer for five tiers is eight distinct paths.

```text
2026-10-27T00:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Loyalty Ladder Path Counter (Climbing Stairs)
2026-10-27T00:50:00Z [INFO] Distinct progression paths to tier 5 = 8
2026-10-27T00:50:00Z [INFO] n=5 → 8
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Climbing Stairs is the gateway dynamic programming problem, and it is just Fibonacci in disguise. The number of distinct ways to reach step i is the number of ways to reach step i minus one, from which you take a single step, plus the number of ways to reach step i minus two, from which you take a double step. Those two sets of paths are disjoint and together cover every possibility, so I add them, giving the recurrence dp of i equals dp of i minus one plus dp of i minus two.

The base cases are one way to be at the ground and one way to reach the first step. Because each value depends only on the previous two, I keep two rolling variables instead of a full array, which gives linear time and constant space.

In my project at National Bank of India, a loyalty ladder let members advance one or two tiers per action, and marketing wanted the count of distinct progression paths to a target tier. This rolling Fibonacci computation answered it instantly, and I noted that a generalized up-to-k-steps variant simply sums the previous k counts and remains linear.
